An abjuration is a formal, solemn, and often public declaration in which a person officially and completely rejects or gives up something they previously believed in, belonged to, or were loyal to — typically under oath.
What makes abjuration different from simply "changing your mind"

If you used to enjoy a TV show and now you don't, that's just a change of taste. No big deal. Abjuration is something far heavier and more deliberate. It is not a quiet, private shift of opinion. It is an announced act — an official declaration made before witnesses, a court, a religious authority, or a governing body. Think of it as signing a binding statement that says: "I hereby formally and permanently reject this."

Three qualities define it. First, it is formal — there is a ceremonial, institutional quality to it; someone in authority is witnessing it. Second, it commonly involves an oath — the person swears (often on a holy text, or before God, or before a court) that they are genuinely and truly abandoning whatever is being renounced. This oath is what gives abjuration its teeth. Third, it is permanent and total — it is not a pause or a hesitation. It is a clean, final severance. The person is declaring they are done, forever.
What kinds of things can be abjured?

Almost anything a person held with deep enough significance that a formal rejection of it carries real weight.

The most classic use historically is the abjuration of a religious belief. During the Middle Ages and the era of the Inquisition, people accused of heresy (beliefs the Church considered false or dangerous) were sometimes forced to make an abjuration — publicly denouncing their "wrong" beliefs and swearing to return to accepted doctrine.

Abjuration also applies to political allegiance. Governments have historically used "Oaths of Abjuration," which were formal documents requiring citizens or subjects to swear they rejected the authority of a particular rival ruler or enemy. Signing such an oath was an act of abjuration — you were cutting your loyalty officially and on the record.

It also applies to a claim to a throne — a king or prince forced to give up his claim to rule would make a formal abjuration of that claim. And in legal contexts, it can apply to citizenship, where renouncing one's nationality before an official body carries the spirit of abjuration.

In short: abjuration is reserved for things that matter — beliefs, loyalties, powers, and identities that carry enough weight that walking away from them requires a solemn public act.

In 1633, the astronomer Galileo Galilei was tried by the Roman Inquisition for supporting the idea that the Earth revolves around the Sun. Faced with the threat of severe punishment, he made a formal abjuration — publicly and officially declaring that he rejected his own scientific findings and accepted the Church's position instead. It was a coerced, agonizing act of official renunciation. A legend (likely invented, but beautifully fitting) says that after kneeling and making his abjuration, he whispered, "And yet it moves."

This example captures everything abjuration is: weighty, official, public, and often tied to an agonizing conflict between inner conviction and external pressure.

Abjuration is never trivial. What is being abandoned is almost always something the person once held with genuine conviction — a faith, a cause, a loyalty. This is exactly why the word appears so often in stories of persecution, coercion, and moral crisis. It places a person at a crossroads: do I stand by what I truly believe, or do I officially declare I don't believe it to survive?

An abjuration made under duress raises a profound question: is it sincere? Historically, many people who were forced to abjure continued secretly holding their original beliefs. This is why courts and religious bodies demanded the abjuration be made publicly and under oath — they wanted to make backing out as difficult and shameful as possible.
How the word is used today

In modern English, "abjuration" lives mainly in formal, legal, historical, and literary writing. You will encounter it in historical accounts of religious persecution, in documents about renouncing citizenship or political allegiance, and in philosophical or literary writing where a weighty, decisive rejection is being described. It is not an everyday conversational word — when someone uses it, they are deliberately signalling that the rejection in question is not casual. It is grave, official, and final.

Here are a few example sentences to make the usage concrete:

"His abjuration of his former beliefs was read aloud before the entire congregation."
"The peace treaty required the abjuration of all territorial claims."
"Galileo's abjuration before the Inquisition remains one of history's most haunting moments of intellectual surrender."
"She filed a formal abjuration of her citizenship, closing the chapter on her previous life entirely."
The single sentence to remember it by

If you want one clean sentence to anchor this word in your memory: An abjuration is a formal, sworn, public act of completely and permanently rejecting something you once believed in or were loyal to — not a quiet change of heart, but an official declaration witnessed and recorded, carrying the full weight of an oath behind it.
